  "text": "The last customer brought a toaster wrapped in a towel.

We had already unplugged the lamps. Dad was taking the brass letters off the shop door, working carefully with a screwdriver too small for the screws.

“Closing down,” I told her.

“I know.” She set the toaster on the counter. “Your father fixed it in 1987.”

Dad put down the screwdriver.

The woman unfolded the towel. One lever was missing its black cap. There was a dent along the side, neatly avoiding the faded inspection sticker.

“Still heats,” she said. “Won’t stay down.”

I looked at the boxes behind us. Forty-three years of spare parts, sorted into things worth selling and things nobody wanted.

Dad pressed the bare lever with his thumb.

“Come back Thursday.”

“We hand over the keys tomorrow,” I said.

He pressed it again.

The woman began wrapping the toaster.

“Never mind. You’ve earned a rest.”

Dad held the towel still.

“Leave it with me.”

After she went, he carried it to the only bench we hadn’t cleared. I found the extension lead while he fetched his glasses from the empty drawer where he always kept them.

For a while I swept around his shoes.

Then he asked for a small spring.

“Which box?”

“The biscuit tin.”

There were six biscuit tins. I opened them one by one.

Outside, the signwriter arrived to measure the window. I let him in and moved our boxes out of his way.

Dad fitted the spring and lowered the lever. This time it stayed.

“Bread?” he asked.

I went to the corner shop and bought a loaf, butter, and two paper plates."
